name: California
blurb: By far the largest U.S. wine producer; Mediterranean climate from cool coastal fog belts to warm inland valleys. Napa and Sonoma lead fine wine; Central Coast, Lodi, and Sierra Foothills add volume and diversity.

name: Oregon
blurb: Cool-climate Willamette Valley is the flagship for Pinot Noir and Chardonnay; warmer southern valleys (Rogue, Umpqua) grow Syrah and Tempranillo.

name: Washington
blurb: Columbia Valley rain shadow: warm, dry growing seasons with cool nights. Cabernet, Merlot, Syrah, and Riesling lead; Walla Walla and Red Mountain are prestige sub-AVAs.

name: New York
blurb: Finger Lakes (Riesling, cool-climate hybrids and vinifera) plus Long Island (maritime Merlot/Cabernet Franc) and Hudson Valley.

name: Virginia
blurb: Humid continental/mid-Atlantic; Viognier is a signature white, with Cabernet Franc, Merlot, and Petit Verdot for reds. Monticello and Shenandoah Valley are key AVAs.

name: Texas
blurb: Hill Country and High Plains dominate plantings; warm, often dry sites favor Tempranillo, Mourvèdre, Cabernet, and Rhône whites. Climate point: Fredericksburg (Hill Country).

name: Michigan
blurb: Lake Michigan moderates Old Mission and Leelanau peninsulas; Riesling, Pinot Gris, and sparkling styles thrive in a cool northern climate.

name: Pennsylvania
blurb: Lake Erie AVA along the shore plus inland Piedmont and Lehigh Valley plantings; hybrids and cool-climate vinifera (Riesling, Cabernet Franc).

name: New Mexico
blurb: High-elevation desert vineyards; historic mission plantings and modern sparkling (e.g. Gruet). Climate point near Mid-Rio Grande / southern growing areas.

name: Idaho
blurb: Snake River Valley AVA shared with Oregon; cool nights and volcanic soils. Riesling, Chardonnay, and Bordeaux/Rhône reds.
